crochet/lemon-peel-stitch.title: Lemon Peel Stitch
crochet/lemon-peel-stitch.content:
As I’ve been getting into crochet, I’ve learned that there are a vast number of kinds of stitches out there to work up fabric from, and there’s not really a standard place documenting all of these. I want to use this garden to start writing down the ones I find. Starting off with the lemon peel stitch, which I used to make a mini scarf out of 50g of yarn I got on sale.
Stitch metrics

Name(s): Lemon Peel
Turning height: 1 ch
Spacing: 2 st
As I continue to document these, I’ll expand on this list of metrics. They’ll be defined here.

Stitch anatomy
A lemon peel stitch is alternating single and double crochet:

[sc, dc]

From what I saw online, every row starts with a single crochet and ends with a double crochet. It likely doesn’t matter because you zigzag back and forth as you work up the fabric, but it helps to remember that to avoid skipping stitches by accident.
Thoughts
For a complete beginner like me, the lemon peel stitch made a great beginner project to work on my consistency with. Nothing’s too complicated and the stitch turned out looking lovely. It seems to be relatively airy as well and drapes solidly (for crochet, at least). It did end up with a flatter texture; I haven’t tried flo/blo variations on it yet, which could convert it into an interesting rib-like fabric.
Swatch instructions

Start by chaining an odd number of stitches (2n+1 where n is the number of stitches desired).
Turn. (The turning stitch was already made.)
Crochet one sc in the 2nd stitch, then one dc in the next, then continue alternating down until the end. You should end in a dc.
Ch 1 and turn.
Repeat 3-4 until done with swatch.

crochet/stitch-metric-definitions.title: Stitch Metric Definitions
crochet/stitch-metric-definitions.content:
Stitch metrics are quantitative descriptors of a stitch that should help describe and categorize it with similar stitches. Crochet isn’t really something you can be 100% quantitative about so there will be some categorical or straight up vibes-based measurements, but the goal is to have reliable data, so I will do my best to only include measurable or at least reasonable metrics.
A lot of these are going to be very straightforward observations that simply don’t get formally put down as their own datapoint. (Turning height is a good example; most patterns will just ask you to ch x and turn inline rather than pointing out the height of the stitch in a preamble). The metrics are, in no particular order:
Name(s)
The names I have seen this stitch referenced as.
Turning height
The number of chains you need to make when turning the stitch. This is mostly equivalent to asking the height of a stitch.
Turning heights often disagree from source to source (for example, hdc is variously noted as a turning height of 1 or 2).
Spacing
The width of a singular stitch, counted in stitches. This is relevant when it comes to determining the length of your base chain: disregarding the turning chain(s), the base chain needs to be divisible by the spacing. For example, you need an even number of chains for lemon peel, so your spacing is 2.
Let s be spacing, t turning height, and n any number. The valid length B of a base chain for any stitch is thus:
B = ns + t
This is, of course, assuming you start with a chain. For a starting chain + row of single crochet, foundation single crochet, or similar starting methods, B=ns. Only once the foundation is done do you then apply the turning height to turn and begin working the stitch.

crochet/suzette-(thicket)-stitch.title: Suzette (Thicket) Stitch
crochet/suzette-(thicket)-stitch.content:
Stitch metrics

Name(s): Suzette, Thicket
Turning height: 1 ch
Spacing: 2
As always, definitions in Stitch Metric Definitions.

Stitch anatomy

[sk, (sc, dc)]

(I’m using the definition here where parentheses mean “work these two into the same stitch.”) This one is very similar to the Lemon Peel Stitch, except that it has each [sc, dc] group go into the same stitch and skips a stitch to keep the same spacing. For this one, the order matters: if you flip the order, the sides will end up zigzagged as each row will end with a space and shift from the one below.
Thoughts
I stitched two test swatches of suzette and lemon peel and compared them to each other. To my eye, the suzette stitch seems to be very slightly more uniform as the double crochets lean into the spaces instead of being squished slightly. It’s an almost imperceptible change, though, so I think it’s a matter of preference which to choose.
Swatch instructions

Start by chaining an odd number of stitches (2n+1 where n is the number of stitches desired).
Turn.
Skip 2nd stitch and crochet sc in 3rd stitch.
Crochet dc in the same stitch, then skip a stitch.
Repeat 3-4 until the end of the row. The row should end in a sc+dc, not a skipped stitch.
Ch 1 and turn.
Repeat 3-6 until done with swatch.
